label: exactgrp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{exactgrp}
Let $M_1\xrightarrow{f_1}M_2\xrightarrow{f_2}M_3\xrightarrow{f_3}M_4$ be an exact sequence of monoids. Suppose that $M_1$ and $M_3$ are groups, then so is $M_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We need to find an inverse for every $m_2\in M_2$. Indeed, the image $m_3:=f_2(m_2)$ of such given $m_2$ is invertible in $M_3$.
Applying $f_3$ we obtain $$e_4=f_3(m_3\cdot m_3^{-1})=f_3( f_2(m_2))\cdot f_3(m_3^{-1})=f_3(m_3^{-1}).$$Therefore, $m_3^{-1}\in\ker(f_3)$ and hence there is $m'_2\in M_2$ such that $f_2(m'_2)=m_3^{-1}$.
It follows that $f_2(m_2\cdot m'_2)=m_3\cdot m_3^{-1}=e_3$, and so there is $m_1\in M_1$ such that $f_1(m_1)=m_2\cdot m'_2$.
Then $$m_2\cdot m'_2\cdot f_1(m_1^{-1})=f_1(m_1)\cdot f_1(m_1^{-1})=e_2,$$
and hence $m'_2\cdot f_1(m_1^{-1})$ is a right inverse of $m_2$. A left inverse is obtained similarly.

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply the $K$-algebra homomorphism \eqref{l} for $g \in G$ and $x\in K$
$$\epsilon_g(x \otimes_k 1)-\epsilon_g(1 \otimes_k\ \phi(g^{})(x)) \mapsto
                                                                                 
                                                                                          
\tilde{\epsilon}_{g^{}}x-\tilde{\epsilon}_{g^{}}x =0.$$
As mentioned above, in the Galois case \eqref{l} is an isomorphism, verifying \eqref{theorth} and consequently \eqref{eq:OI}.
                                                                                                              
For the last claim of the lemma, let $\epsilon_g' \in K \otimes_k K$ be an idempotent for some $g\in G$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eps'}
\epsilon_g'(x \otimes_k 1) = \epsilon_g'(1 \otimes_k \phi(g^{})(x)),\ \forall x \in K.
\end{equation}
                                          
By \eqref{eq:OI} there exist $a_{h} \in K$ for every $h\in G$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{epsum}
\epsilon_g' = \sum\limits_{h \in G}\epsilon_{h}(a_{h} \otimes_k 1).
\end{equation}
Thus, by the assumption \eqref{eps'}     
we obtain
$$\sum\limits_{h \in G}\epsilon_{h}(a_{h} \otimes_k 1)((x \otimes_k 1)-(1 \otimes_k \phi(g^{})(x))) =\epsilon_g'((x \otimes_k 1)-(1 \otimes_k \phi(g^{})(x)))= 0,\ \forall x \in K.$$
Applying the isomorphism \eqref{l}, with the orthogonality of $\{\tilde{\epsilon}_g\}_{g\in G}$ in mind, yields
$$\sum\limits_{h\in G}\tilde{\epsilon}_{h^{}}a_{h}(x-\phi(h^{-1}g)(x)) = 0,\ \forall x \in K.$$
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq2}
a_{h}(x-\phi(h^{-1}g)(x))= 0,\ \forall h \in G, x\in K.\end{equation}

By the Galois assumption (see Definition \ref{Galdef}) it follows
that $a_{h} = 0$ for every $h \neq g$, otherwise there exists
$y\in K$ such that $y -\phi(h^{-1}g)(y) $ does not belong to some
maximal ideal containing Ann$_K(a_{h})$ and, particularly, does
not annihilate $a_h$ contradicting \eqref{eq2} for $h$.
Therefore,                                                 
\eqref{epsum} is just $\epsilon_g' = \epsilon_g(a_g \otimes_k 1)$.
Applying the isomorphism \eqref{l} once again on $\epsilon_g'^2=\epsilon_g'$ shows $a_g$ is an idempotent in $K$, and hence the claim.

label: Defact
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Defact}
Let a groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ act on a set $A$ as above.
Suppose that both $\mathcal{G}$ and $A$ admit monoidal products $\otimes$ and $\otimes_A$ respectively, where the monoidal structure of $\mathcal{G}$ is strict.
We say that $\mathcal{G}$ acts on $A$ as a monoidal groupoid if  the anchor $\varsigma:A\to{\text {ob}(\mathcal{G})}$ is a monoid homomorphism, and the rules\\
$\begin{array}{ccc}
\text {ob}(A^\mathcal{G})\times\text {ob}(A^\mathcal{G})&\to&\text {ob}(A^\mathcal{G})\\
(a,b)&\mapsto& a\otimes_A b
\end{array}$\ and\
$\begin{array}{ccc}
\hom(A^\mathcal{G})\times\hom(A^\mathcal{G})&\to&\hom(A^\mathcal{G})\\
(f,g)&\mapsto& f\otimes g
\end{array}$\\
determine a bifunctor $A^\mathcal{G}\times A^\mathcal{G}\to A^\mathcal{G}$, enriching the action groupoid $A^\mathcal{G}$ with a monoidal structure.

\label{cliffextdef}                       
(\textit{i}) A $k$-algebra homomorphism
$\psi_G : A_G \rightarrow A'_G$ between two strongly $G$-graded $k$-algebras
\begin{equation}\label{AA'}
A_G = \bigoplus_{g \in G}A_g \text{ and }A'_G =  \bigoplus_{g \in G}A_g'
\end{equation}
                                                      
is a \textit{graded homomorphism} if $\psi_G(A_g) = A'_g$ for every $g \in G$.
The graded algebras \eqref{AA'} are \textit{graded isomorphic}, and written $A_G\stackrel{G}\cong A'_G$, if there exists a graded isomorphism between them.

extension} of $R$ is a pair $(A_G,\iota)$ where $A_G$ is a strongly
$G$-graded $k$-algebra \eqref{eq:D:1} and $\iota : R \to A_G$ is a
$k$-algebra embedding with $\iota(R) = A_e$.
                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                              
Two $G$-graded Clifford
system extensions $(A_G,\iota)$ and $(A'_G,\iota')$ of $R$ are equivalent if
there exists a graded isomorphism $\psi_G : A_G \xrightarrow{G} A'_G $ such
that $\psi_G\circ \iota = \iota'$. Denote the equivalence class of $(A_G,\iota)$  by $[(A_G,\iota)]$.

label: HdRlemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{HdRlemma}
The rule \eqref{actrule} determines a well-defined $\mathcal{MC}'_K$-action on $\text{Cliff}_k(G,C(K))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove that \eqref{actrule} is well-defined, let $[(B_G,\iota)]=[(B'_G,\iota')]\in\mbox{Cliff}_k (G, R)$, and let $[P]=[P'] \in {\text{Mod}}^*(R'\text{-} R)$.
We claim that $[(P(B_G),P(\iota))]=[(P'(B'_G),P'(\iota'))]$ (compare with \cite[Lemma 2.6]{JHDR}).
Indeed, let $\lambda: P \stackrel{\cong}{\to} P'$ be an $S\text{-} R$ bimodule isomorphism admitting a dual $R\text{-} R'$ bimodule isomorphism
${\lambda}^*: \begin{array}{rcl}\check{P'} &\to &\check{P}\\
f'&\mapsto & f'\circ\lambda\end{array}$.
Next, let $\psi_G: B_G \stackrel{G}{\to} B_G'$ be a $G$-graded $k$-algebra isomorphism
giving rise to an equivalence of the above Clifford system extensions of $R$, i.e. satisfying $\psi\circ \iota = \iota'$.
Then a direct computation yields that
$$P(\psi) :\begin{array}{rcl}
P(B_G)&\to &{P'}({B'}_G)\\
p \otimes_R b_g\otimes_R f&\mapsto & \lambda(p) \otimes_R \psi_G(b_g)\otimes_R {\lambda^*}^{-1}(f)
\end{array},\ \forall g \in G, b_g \in B_g, p \in P, f \in \check{P}$$
is a $G$-graded $k$-algebra isomorphism satisfying $P(\psi)\circ P(\iota) = P'(\iota')$, that is an equivalence of
$(P(B_G),P(\iota))$ and $(P'({B'_G}),P'({\iota'}))$ as Clifford system $R'$-extensions.



Now, for any Clifford system extension class $[(B_G,\iota)])\in\mbox{Cliff}_k (G, R)$ and two composable morphisms (see \eqref{compmods})
$[_{R'}P_{R}],[_{R''}P'_{R'}]\in\text{hom}({\mathcal{MC}'_K)}$,
the rule
$$ \begin{array}{ccc}
(P'\otimes_{R'} P)\big{(}B_G\big{)}& \to& (P'(P(B_G))\\
(p' \otimes_{R'} p)\otimes_R b_g \otimes_R (f \otimes_{R'} f')& \mapsto& p' \otimes_{R'}(p \otimes_R b_g \otimes_R f)\otimes_{R'} f',
\end{array}$$
for $f'\in \check{P'}, f \in \check{P}, p \in P, p' \in P'$, and $b_g \in B_g$ determines an isomorphism of $G$-graded $k$-algebras,
which respects the corresponding embeddings $(P'\otimes_{R'}P)(\iota)$ and $P'(P(\iota))$.
It follows that
$$([P'\otimes_{R'}P]([(B_G,\iota)]) = [P']([P]([(B_G,\iota)]))\in\mbox{Cliff}_k (G, R'')$$
(see \cite[Lemma 2.7]{JHDR}), that is $\mathcal{MC}'_K$ acts on $\text{Cliff}_k(G,C(K))$ as a groupoid.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $ [M_g]:=\Phi(g) \in \text{Pic}_k(R)$ for every $g \in G$.
Since $\Phi$ is a group homomorphism, there exist (non-unique) $R$-bimodule isomorphisms
$$\Gamma_{g,h} : M_g \otimes_R M_h \to M_{gh},\ \  \forall g,h \in G,$$
which yield the 3-cocycle $T=T^{\Phi}:G^3\to K^*$ satisfying (see \cite[(11)]{CG})
\begin{equation}\label{T(g,h,t)}
\Gamma_{gh,t}(\Gamma_{g,h} \otimes_R M_t) = T_{g,h,t}\cdot\Gamma_{g,ht}(M_g \otimes_R \Gamma_{h,t}),\ \  \forall g,h,t\in G.
\end{equation}
Next, set $r(f,p):=\tau_P(f \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p)\in R$ for $\tau_P$ as in  \eqref{nuP}, and let
$$ \Gamma_{g,h}^P:
\begin{array}{ccc}
P(M_g) \otimes_S P(M_h)&\to & P(M_{gh})\\
(p_1 \otimes_{R} a_g \otimes_R f_1) \otimes_S(p_2 \otimes_{R} a_h \otimes_R f_2) &\mapsto &
p_1 \otimes_{R} \Gamma_{g,h}(a_gr(f_1, p_2)\otimes_R a_h) \otimes_R f_2,
\end{array}
$$
for every $f_1,f_2 \in \check{P}, p_1,p_2 \in P, a_g \in M_g,\ a_h \in M_h$.
It is not hard to verify that for all $g,h \in G$, the maps $ \Gamma_{g,h}^P$ are isomorphisms of $S$-bimodules. Let us inspect their corresponding 3-cocycle. Let
$$x_g = p_1 \otimes_{R} a_g \otimes_{R} f_1\in P(M_g),\ x_h = p_2 \otimes_{R} a_h \otimes_{R} f_2\in P(M_h),\ x_t = p_3 \otimes_{R} a_t \otimes_{R} f_3\in P(M_t),$$
where $a_g \in M_g, a_h \in M_h,a_t \in M_t,$ and $p_i \in P, f_i \in \check{P}$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$. Then we have
\begin{align*}
&\Gamma_{gh,t}^P(\Gamma_{g,h}^P(x_g \otimes_S x_h)\otimes_S x_t)\\
=&\ \Gamma_{gh,t}^P((p_1\otimes_{R}\Gamma_{g,h}(a_g\tau_P(f_1 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_2) \otimes_R a_h)\otimes_R f_2) \otimes_S (p_3 \otimes_{R} a_t \otimes_{R} f_3))\\
=&\  p_1\otimes_{R} \Gamma_{gh,t}(\Gamma_{g,h}(a_g\tau_P(f_1 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_2) \otimes_R a_h)\tau_P(f_2 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_3)\otimes_R a_t)\otimes_R f_3 \cdots
\end{align*}
applying \eqref{T(g,h,t)} yields
\begin{align*}
\cdots=& \  p_1\otimes_R T_{g,h,t}\cdot\Gamma_{g,ht}(a_g f_1(p_2) \otimes_R \Gamma_{h,t}(a_hf_2(p_3)\otimes_R a_t))\otimes_R f_3\\
=& \ T_{g,h,t}\cdot(p_1\otimes_{R}\Gamma_{g,ht}(a_g \tau_P(f_1 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_2) \otimes_R \Gamma_{h,t}(a_h\tau_P(f_2 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_3)\otimes_R a_t))\otimes_R f_3)\\
=&\ T_{g,h,t}\cdot\Gamma_{g,ht}^P(x_g \otimes_S (p_2 \otimes_{R} \Gamma_{h,t}(a_h \tau_P(f_2 \otimes_{{\text{end}}_R(P)} p_3) \otimes_R a_t) \otimes_R f_3))\\
=&\ T_{g,h,t}\cdot\Gamma_{g,ht}^P(x_g \otimes_S \Gamma_{h,t}^P(x_h \otimes_S x_t)).
\end{align*}
Consequently, $T^{P(\Phi)}=T^{\Phi}\in Z^3(G,K^*)$ and thus $\tilde{T}_{\phi}(P(\Phi))= \tilde{T}_{\phi}(\Phi)$.

label: cocy
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M$ be a left $K_{\phi}G$-module such that ${\text{res}}([M])=[K]$.
Then there exists an isomorphism $\varphi:K\xrightarrow{\cong} M$ of $K$-modules. For every $g\in G$ let
$$\varphi_g:=\varphi^{-1}(u_g\star\varphi(1))\in K.$$

\textit{Step 1.} For every $g\in G$, the element $\varphi_g$ is invertible. Moreover,\begin{eqnarray}\label{cocy}\pi_{{\varphi}}=\pi_{M,\varphi}:\begin{array}{ccc}
G&\to& K^*\\
g&\mapsto &\varphi_g
\end{array}\end{eqnarray}
is a 1-cocycle, where the $G$-module structure of $K^*$ is via $\phi$.

\textit{Proof of Step 1.}
For every $g,h\in G$
\begin{eqnarray}\label{1cc}\begin{array}{rl}
\varphi_{gh}&=\varphi^{-1}(u_{gh}\star\varphi(1))=\varphi^{-1}(u_gu_h\star\varphi(1))=\varphi^{-1}(u_g\star(u_h\star\varphi(1)))\\
&=\varphi^{-1}(u_g\star\varphi(\varphi_h))=\varphi^{-1}(u_g\star(\varphi_h\cdot\varphi(1)))=\varphi^{-1}(u_g\cdot \varphi_h\star(\varphi(1)))\\
&=\varphi^{-1}(g(\varphi_h)\cdot u_g\star(\varphi(1)))=g(\varphi_h)\cdot \varphi^{-1}(u_g\star(\varphi(1)))=g(\varphi_h)\cdot \varphi_g.
\end{array}\end{eqnarray}
Since $\varphi_e=1$, putting $h=g^{-1}$ in \eqref{1cc} we deduce that $\varphi_g\in K^*$ for every $g\in G$.
In fact, \eqref{1cc} says that $g\mapsto \varphi_g$
                                                                                                                                        
is a 1-cocycle.

\textit{Step 2.} With the notation \eqref{cocy}, the rule $[M]\mapsto [\pi_{M,\varphi}]$ determines a well-defined map $\ker({\text{res}})\to H^1(G,K^*_{\phi})$.

\textit{Proof of Step 2.} We show that the cohomology class
$[\pi_{M,{\varphi}}]\in H^1(G,K^*_{\phi})$ neither depends on the representative $M\in [M]$, nor on the isomorphism $\varphi$.
Indeed, let $M$ and $\tilde{M}$ be left $K_{\phi}G$-modules via the actions $``\star"$ and $``\tilde{\star}"$ respectively, such that $[M]=[\tilde{M}] \in \ker({\text{res}})$,
and let $\lambda:M \stackrel{\cong}\rightarrow \tilde{M}$ be a $K_{\phi}G$-module isomorphism.
In particular, for every $g\in G$ and $m\in M$
\begin{equation}\label{lamb}
\lambda(u_g\star m)=u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda(m).
\end{equation}
                                                                                                  
Let
\begin{equation}\label{varphitilde}
{\varphi}:K\xrightarrow{\cong} M,\ \ \ \tilde{\varphi}:K\xrightarrow{\cong} \tilde{M}\end{equation}
be $K$-module isomorphisms determining the corresponding 1-cocycles
$\pi_{M,{\varphi}}$ and $\pi_{\tilde{M},\tilde{\varphi}}$ as in \eqref{cocy}.
We claim that these 1-cocycles defer by the 1-coboundary
$$g\mapsto g(x)\cdot x^{-1},\text{  where  } x:=\varphi^{-1}\circ\lambda^{-1}\circ\tilde{\varphi}(1)\in K^*.$$
First, since $\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi$ is a $K$-morphism we have
$$x\cdot(\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi( 1))=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi( x\cdot 1)=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi( x)
=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi(\varphi^{-1}\circ\lambda^{-1}\circ\tilde{\varphi}(1))=1,$$
hence $\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi( 1)=x^{-1}.$
Next, for every $g\in G$
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\tilde{\varphi}_g&=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\tilde{\star}\tilde{\varphi}(1))=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda\circ\varphi\circ\varphi^{-1}\circ\lambda^{-1}\circ\tilde{\varphi}(1))\\
&=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda\circ\varphi((\varphi^{-1}\circ\lambda^{-1}\circ\tilde{\varphi}(1))\cdot 1))
=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda(\varphi(x\cdot 1)))=\cdots
\end{array}$$
The element $x\in K$ can be pulled out of the $K$-morphism $\varphi$, thus
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\cdots&=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda(x\cdot\varphi( 1)))=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g\cdot x\tilde{\star}\lambda(\varphi( 1)))
                                              
=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(g(x)\cdot u_g\tilde{\star}\lambda(\varphi( 1)))=\cdots
\end{array}$$
By \eqref{lamb}
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\cdots&=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(g(x)\cdot \lambda(u_g\star\varphi( 1)))=g(x)\cdot\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}( \lambda(u_g\star\varphi( 1)))=g(x)\cdot\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}( \lambda(\varphi( \varphi_g)))\\
&=g(x)\cdot\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}( \lambda(\varphi( \varphi_g\cdot 1)))=\cdots
\end{array}$$
Again, pull $\varphi_g\in K$ out of the $K$-morphism $\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ\lambda\circ \varphi$ and apply the above description of $x^{-1}$ to obtain
$$\cdots=g(x)\cdot\varphi_g\cdot(\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}\circ \lambda\circ \varphi( 1))=g(x)\cdot\varphi_g\cdot x^{-1}.$$
We conclude that $\tilde{\varphi}_g\cdot\varphi_g^{-1}=g(x)\cdot x^{-1}$
and hence we are done.

\textit{Step 3.}
The well-defined map
\begin{equation}\label{Pi-1}\begin{array}{ccc}\ker({\text{res}})&\to& H^1(G,K_{\phi}^*)\\~[M]&\mapsto &[\pi_{M,\varphi}]\end{array}
\end{equation} is a group homomorphism.

\textit{Proof of Step 3.}
Let $M$ and $\tilde{M}$ be (not necessarily isomorphic) left $K_{\phi}G$-modules such that $[M],[\tilde{M}] \in \ker({\text{res}})$.
Let \eqref{varphitilde} be $K$-module isomorphisms determining the corresponding 1-cocycles
$\pi_{M,{\varphi}}$ and $\pi_{\tilde{M},\tilde{\varphi}}$ as in \eqref{cocy}.
Let us compute the 1-cocycle
$$\pi_{M\otimes_K\tilde{M},\hat{\varphi}}:G\to K^*$$
with respect to the $K$-module isomorphism
\begin{eqnarray}\label{cocytens}\hat{\varphi}:\begin{array}{ccc}
K&\to& M\otimes_K\tilde{M}\\
x&\mapsto &\varphi(1)\otimes_K\tilde{\varphi}(x)
\end{array}.\end{eqnarray}
By the rule in step 1 (see \eqref{cocy}) applied on \eqref{cocytens}, and the $K_{\phi}G$-action \eqref{tensrepr} on the tensor product, we have for every $g\in G$
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\pi_{M\otimes_K\tilde{M},\hat{\varphi}}(g)&=\hat{\varphi}_g=\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g(\hat{\varphi}(1)))=\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g(\varphi(1)\otimes_K\tilde{\varphi}(1)))\\
&=\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(u_g*\varphi(1)\otimes_Ku_g\tilde{*}\tilde{\varphi}(1))=\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(\varphi(\varphi_g)\otimes_K \tilde{\varphi}(\tilde{\varphi}_g))\\
&=\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(\varphi(\varphi_g\cdot 1)\otimes_K \tilde{\varphi}(\tilde{\varphi}_g))=\varphi_g\cdot\hat{\varphi}^{-1}(\varphi( 1)\otimes_K \tilde{\varphi}(\tilde{\varphi}_g))\\
&=\varphi_g\cdot\tilde{\varphi}_g=\pi_{M,{\varphi}}(g)\cdot\pi_{\tilde{M},\tilde{\varphi}}(g).
\end{array}$$
In particular, the $H^1(G,K^*_{\phi})$-classes $[\pi_{M\otimes_K\tilde{M},\hat{\varphi}}]$ and $[\pi_{M,{\varphi}}]\cdot[\pi_{\tilde{M},\tilde{\varphi}}]$ are equal, proving the homomorphism property.

\textit{Step 4. The map \eqref{Pi-1} is an isomorphism.}

\textit{Proof of Step 4.}
Here is a construction of the inverse of the group homomorphism \eqref{Pi-1}.
We endow the trivial element in Mod$(K)$, that is free $K$-module of rank 1, with a left $K_{\phi}G$-action for
a given 1-cocycle $\pi:G\to K^*_{\phi}$ as follows.
                                                                                                                                              
\begin{equation}\label{act*}(\sum_{g\in G}x_gu_g)\star x:=\sum_{g\in G}x_g\cdot\pi(g)\cdot g(x),\ \ \ \ \sum_{g\in G}x_gu_g\in K_{\phi}G,\ x\in K_{\pi}.\end{equation}
                                                                 
Then it is not hard to verify, using the 1-cocycle condition, that \eqref{act*} indeed describes a left $K_{\phi}G$-module on $K$.
Denote this module by $K_{\pi}$.

Furthermore, if $[\pi]=[\hat{\pi}]\in H^1(G,K^*_{\phi})$ then the corresponding $K_{\phi}G$-modules $K_{\pi}$ and $K_{\hat{\pi}}$ are isomorphic as follows.
The fact that the 1-cocycles are cohomologically equivalent says that there exists $y\in K^*$ such that
$$\pi(g)=y^{-1}\cdot g(y)\cdot \hat{\pi}(g),\ \ \ \forall g\in G.$$
Then it is easily checked that $\begin{array}{ccc}K_{\pi}&\to &K_{\hat{\pi}}\\ x&\mapsto& y\cdot x\end{array}$ is a $K_{\phi}G$-module isomorphism.
In other words, there is a well-defined map
\begin{equation}\label{piphi}
H^1(G,K_{\phi}^*)\to \ker({\text{res}}).\end{equation}
To conclude the proof, the fact that \eqref{piphi} is indeed the inverse of the group homomorphism \eqref{Pi-1} is left to the reader.

label: psigdef
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M$ be a left $K_{\phi}G$-module.
To show that ${\text{res}}([M])$ is $G$-invariant we need to present a $K$-module isomorphism between $$g(M)=_{\phi(g^{-1})}K_1 \otimes_K M \otimes_K \ _{\phi(g)}K_1$$ (see \eqref{Gactmd})
and $M$ for every $g\in G$.
                                                                             
Indeed, let
\begin{eqnarray}\label{psigdef}\psi_g :\begin{array}{ccc}g(M) &\rightarrow& M\\
x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y& \mapsto& g(x)\cdot y\cdot u_g\star m
\end{array},\ \ x,y \in K,m \in M.\end{eqnarray}
We first check that $\psi_g$ agrees with the different actions of $K$ on the three components of $g(M)$. Note that any $z \in K$ and $x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y$ in the module $g(M)$ satisfy
$$\begin{array}{rl}
z(x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y)&=g^{-1}(z)\cdot x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y\\ &= x\otimes_K\ {g^{-1}}(z)m \otimes_K y = x\otimes_K m\otimes_K {g^{-1}}(z) (y)\\&=x\otimes_K m \otimes_K z\cdot y.
\end{array}$$
Applying $\psi_g$ on each of the above yields
\begin{equation}\label{difact}z\cdot g(x)\cdot y\cdot u_g\star m,\end{equation} and so $\psi_g$ is well-defined. Moreover, since \eqref{difact} is equal to $z(\psi_g(x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y)),$
                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                     
it follows that $\psi_g$ is a homomorphism of $K$-modules.
To show that $\psi_g$ is invertible let
$$\psi'_g :\begin{array}{ccc}M &\rightarrow& g(M)\\
m&\mapsto& 1 \otimes_K\ u_g^{-1}\star m \otimes_K 1\end{array}.$$
Then, for every $g\in G, m\in M$ and $x,y\in K$ we have
$$\psi'_g(\psi_g(x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y)) = \psi'_g( g(x)\cdot y\cdot u_g\star m) = 1 \otimes_K x\cdot g^{-1}(y)m \otimes_K 1 = x \otimes_K m \otimes_K y.$$
On the other hand
$$\psi_g(\psi'_g(m))=\psi_g(1 \otimes_K\ u_g^{-1}\star m \otimes_K 1)=m.$$
Therefore, $\psi'_g=(\psi_g)^{-1}$, and so $g(M) \cong M$, proving the claim.

body_md:
\label{exactPKG}
With the notations \eqref{alpha3} and \eqref{alpha2}, the sequence
$${\text{Ext}{(\phi,\text{Pic}(K))}}\xrightarrow{\alpha_2}\text{Pic}(K)^{\phi}\xrightarrow{\alpha_3} H^2(G,K^*_{\phi})$$

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $[P]\in$Im$(\alpha_2)=$Im$({\text{res}})\cap$Pic$(K)$. Then we regard $[P]$ as a left $K_{\phi}G$-module. Apply the set $B_P$ of left $K$-module isomorphisms \eqref{BP} putting $P$ for $M$
(as proven in Lemma \ref{resext} these isomorphisms realize the invariance of $[P]$).
With the notation of \S\ref{alpha3sect}, the corresponding set of maps $\{\tilde{\psi}_g : P \rightarrow P\}_{g\in G}$ are given by
$$\tilde{\psi}_g(p) :=u_g*p,\ \  g\in G, p\in P$$ and satisfy \eqref{tildepsi}.
By the definition \eqref{alpha3} $$\alpha_3([P]) = [c_{B_P}]\in H^2(G,K^*),$$ where $c_{B_P}(g,h) = \tilde{\psi}_{gh}\circ\tilde{\psi}_{h}^{-1}\circ\tilde{\psi}_{g}^{-1}$.
But for every $g,h\in G$ and $p\in P$
$$\tilde{\psi}_{gh}(\tilde{\psi}_{h}^{-1}(\tilde{\psi}_{g}^{-1}(p)))=u_{gh}\cdot u_h^{-1}\cdot u_g^{-1}*p=p,$$
and so $c_{B_P}(g,h) =1$. Therefore, $[P] \in \ker(\alpha_3)$.

On the other hand, let $[P] \in \ker(\alpha_3)$. Since $P$ is $G$-invariant there exists a set $\{\tilde{\psi}_g\}_{g\in G}: P \rightarrow P$ of bijections satisfying \eqref{tildepsi}.
                                                      
Moreover, since $\alpha_3([P])$ is cohomologically trivial, there exist elements $\{\lambda_{g}\}_{g\in G} \in K^*$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{tildemult}
\tilde{\psi}_{gh}\circ\tilde{\psi}_h^{-1}\circ\tilde{\psi}_g^{-1} = \lambda_{gh}\cdot\lambda_{g}^{-1}\cdot g(\lambda_{h}^{-1}),\ \  \forall g,h \in G.\end{equation}
Then $P$ can be furnished with a left $K_{\phi}G$-module structure by defining
$$u_g*p := \lambda_g^{-1}\cdot\tilde{\psi_g}(p),\ \ \forall g \in G, p \in P.$$
Indeed, by \eqref{tildemult} we deduce that for every $g,h \in G$ and $p \in P$
$$u_{gh}*p =\lambda_{gh}^{-1}\cdot\tilde{\psi}_{gh}(p) =
                                                                                                                                     
\lambda_g^{-1}\cdot g(\lambda_h^{-1})\cdot\tilde{\psi}_g\circ\tilde{\psi}_h(p)=\lambda_g^{-1}\cdot\tilde{\psi}_g(\lambda_h^{-1}\tilde{\psi}_h(p))=u_g*(u_h*p).$$
Therefore, $[P]$ belongs to the image of \eqref{resmap}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The fact that \eqref{prepsi} is well-defined is clear.
Next, the Galois setting yields an isomorphism of $K$-modules (see \cite[IV(2.1)]{FDEI})
\begin{equation}\label{theta2}K \otimes_k M^{\phi} \cong M. \end{equation}
By \eqref{theta2} we deduce that for every $[M_1],[M_2] \in{\text{Mod}}(K_{\phi}G)$
                                                                          
\begin{eqnarray}\label{eqarr}\begin{array}{rl}
K \otimes_k M_1^{\phi} \otimes_k M_2^{\phi} \cong& K \otimes_k M_1^{\phi} \otimes_K K \otimes_k M_2^{\phi}\\
\cong& M_1 \otimes_K M_2 \\
\cong& K \otimes_k (M_1\otimes_K M_2)^{\phi}.
\end{array}\end{eqnarray}
By the Galois assumption, $K$ is a $k$-progenerator. This property allows us to cancel out $K\otimes_k-$ on both hands of \eqref{eqarr} \cite[I, Prop. 3.3]{FDEI} so as to obtain a $k$-module isomorphism
$$(M_1\otimes_K M_2)^{\phi} \cong M_1^{\phi} \otimes_k M_2^{\phi}, $$
thereby proving that \eqref{prepsi} is a group homomorphism. To complete the proof, here is an inverse of \eqref{prepsi}
\begin{eqnarray}\label{prepsiinv}                  
\begin{array}{ccc}
{\text{Mod}} (k) &\rightarrow& {\text{Mod}}(K_{\phi}G)\\
~[P] &\mapsto& [K\otimes_kP]\end{array},\end{eqnarray}
where the the $K_{\phi}G$-module $K \otimes_k P$, whose $G$-module action is given by
$$u_g*(x \otimes_k p) :=\ \phi(g)(x)\otimes_k p, \ \ \ x \in K, p \in P,g \in G.$$
Indeed, \eqref{theta2} ascertains that \eqref{prepsiinv} is a left inverse of \eqref{prepsi}.
Conversely, by putting $M:=K \otimes_k P,\ \ [P]\in {\text{Mod}} (k)$ in \eqref{theta2}, we have
$$K \otimes_k (K \otimes_k P)^{\phi} \cong K\otimes_k P, \ \  [P]\in {\text{Mod}} (k).$$
By the $k$-progenerator property of $K$, this further yields $(K \otimes_k P)^{\phi} \cong P$, proving that \eqref{prepsiinv} is also a right inverse of \eqref{prepsi}, and hence the claim.

$$ \begin{array}{ll}
  \mu'(p_1\otimes_K a_gu_g \otimes_K f_1)\circ\mu'(p_2\otimes_K a_hu_h \otimes f_2)(p)& = \mu'(p_1\otimes_K a_gu_g \otimes_K f_1)(a_h\cdot{\phi(h)}(f_2(p))\star p_2)
  \\ &=a_g\cdot{\phi(g)}(f_1(a_h\cdot{\phi(h)}(f_2(p))\star p_2))\star p_1\cdots\end{array}$$
                                                
Since scalars from $K$ can be pulled out of $f_1 \in$ Hom$_K(P,K)$, we obtain
  \begin{align*}\cdots
  =& a_g\cdot{\phi(g)}(a_h)\cdot{\phi(g)}(f_1(p_2))\cdot{\phi(gh)}(f_2(p))\star p_1\\=& \mu'(p_1 \otimes_K a_g\cdot{\phi(g)}(a_h)\cdot{\phi(g)}(f_1(p_2))u_{gh} \otimes_K f_2)(p)\\
  =&  \mu'((p_1\otimes_K a_gu_g \otimes_K f_1)\cdot(p_2\otimes_K a_hu_h \otimes_K f_2))(p),
  \end{align*}
where the last equality follows from the multiplication rule in $P(K_{\phi}G)$ \eqref{mult}. Thus, $\mu'$ respects composition in ${\text{end}}_k(P)$,
evaluated on every element $p\in P$, and is hence multiplicative.

Let us first show that $\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i \otimes_k 1)$
is an idempotent which satisfies an appropriate equation of the form \eqref{theorth}. We compute
$$\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i \otimes_k 1)\sum\limits_j(a^g_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_j \otimes_k 1)=
\sum\limits_{i,j}(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_ia^g_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_j \otimes_k 1)=\cdots$$
since $b^g_ia^g_j \in A_e= K$ commutes with $\epsilon_h$ we obtain
$$\cdots=\sum\limits_{i,j}(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)(a^g_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h^2(b^g_j \otimes_k 1)=\sum\limits_j(a^g_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_j \otimes_k 1).$$
                                                                                                                                                                    
Therefore, $\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i \otimes_k 1)\in K \otimes_k K$ is an idempotent for every $g,h\in G$.
We next check condition \eqref{theorth}. For $x \in K$ we have
$$\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i \otimes_k 1)(x\otimes_k 1) = \sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_ix\otimes_k 1)=\cdots$$
since $b^g_i \in A_{g}$ we have $b^g_ix = \phi(g)(x)b^g_i$ (see \eqref{commrule}), and hence
$$\cdots=\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(\phi(g)(x)\otimes_k 1)(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)=\cdots$$
                                                                                                                                      
using the rule \eqref{theorth} properly we obtain
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\cdots &=\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(1\otimes_k\phi(h)(\phi(g)(x)))(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)\\
 &=\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(x))(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)\\ &=\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(x)).
\end{array}$$
                                                                                                                          
Thus, for every $g,h\in G$ and $x\in K$, the idempotent $\epsilon'({g,h}):=\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)\in K\otimes_kK$ satisfies
$$\epsilon'(g,h)(x\otimes_k 1)=\epsilon'(g,h)(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(x)).$$
The third claim in Lemma \ref{L:2.2} implies that for every $g,h \in G$ there exists an idempotent $a(g,h)\in K$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{epsil'}
\epsilon'(g,h)=\epsilon_{hg}(a(g,h)\otimes_k1)=\epsilon_{hg}(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(a(g,h))).
\end{equation}
To prove (the left equality in) \eqref{Miyash}, it is enough to show that $a(g,h)\stackrel{?}{=}1$ for all $g,h\in G$.
Indeed, multiply \eqref{epsil'} by $a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1$ from the left and by $b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1$ from the right,
and sum up over $j$ having
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\sum\limits_j(a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon'(g,h)(b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)&=\sum\limits_j(a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_{hg}(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(a(g,h)))(b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\\
&=\sum\limits_j(a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_{hg}(b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(a(g,h)))=\\
&=\epsilon'(g^{-1},hg)(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(a(g,h)))=\cdots
\end{array}$$
Applying \eqref{epsil'} for $\epsilon'(g^{-1},hg)
                                                                                 
$ yields an idempotent $a(g^{-1},hg)\in K$ with
\begin{eqnarray}\label{onehand}\begin{array}{rl}
\cdots&=\epsilon_h(a(g^{-1},hg)\otimes_k1)(1\otimes_k\phi(hg)(a(g,h)))\\
&=\epsilon_h(a(g^{-1},hg)\phi(g)(a(g,h))\otimes_k1).
\end{array}\end{eqnarray}
On the other hand,
$$\begin{array}{rl}
\sum\limits_j(a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon'(g,h)(b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)&=\sum\limits_j(a^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)
\sum\limits_i(a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_i\otimes_k 1)(b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\\
&=\sum\limits_{i,j}(a^{g^{-1}}_j a^g_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h(b^g_ib^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)=\cdots
\end{array}$$
Since $a^{g^{-1}}_j a^g_i,b^g_ib^{g^{-1}}_j\in K$ for every $i,j$, they all commute with $\epsilon_h$. We conclude
$$\cdots=\sum\limits_{i,j}(a^{g^{-1}}_j a^g_i \otimes_k 1)(b^g_ib^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_h
=\sum\limits_{j}(a^{g^{-1}}_j(\sum\limits_{i} a^g_i b^g_i)b^{g^{-1}}_j \otimes_k 1){\bf \textcolor{violet}{)}}\epsilon_h=\epsilon_h.$$
Comparing with \eqref{onehand} we have $\epsilon_h(a(g^{-1},hg)\phi(g)(a(g,h))\otimes_k1)=\epsilon_h.$
Then Lemma \ref{Kidem} says that the idempotents $a(g,h)\in K$ are invertible and thus equal to 1 for every $g,h\in G$,
                                                                             
verifying (the left equality in) \eqref{Miyash}.
At this point we promptly make use of \eqref{Miyash} to get
$$
(c_{g}\otimes_{k}1)\epsilon_{hg}=(c_{g}\otimes_{k}1)\sum\limits_i(a^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_{h}(b^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)
=\sum\limits_{i}(c_{g}a^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)\epsilon_{h}(b^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)=\cdots
$$
Assuming that $c_g\in A_g$, we have $c_{g}a^{g}_i\in K$ and so
$$\cdots=\sum\limits_{i}\epsilon_{h}(c_{g}a^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)(b^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)
=\sum\limits_{i}\epsilon_{h}(c_{g}\otimes_k 1)(a^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)(b^{g}_i \otimes_k 1)=\epsilon_{h}(c_{g}\otimes_k 1),$$
verifying (the left equality in) \eqref{pass}.
Finally, sum up either one of the equalities in \eqref{Miyash} over all $g\in G$ to establish that
$$1 \otimes_k 1=\sum\limits_{g\in G}\epsilon_{hg}=\sum\limits_{g\in G}\epsilon_{gh}\in (A_G \otimes_k A'_G)\epsilon_h (A_G \otimes_k A'_G),$$
and by that to deduce \eqref{prefull}.

body_md:
Let $[A_G],[A'_G]\in\text{Cliff}_k(\phi,K)$.
                                                 
Implementing Theorem \ref{L:2.4} we have
$$\rho'_{\phi}([A_G]\cdot[A_G])=\rho'_{\phi}([A_G\otimes_{\phi}A'_G])=[A_G\otimes_{\phi}A'_G]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}=[\epsilon(A_G\otimes_{k}A'_G)\epsilon]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}=\ldots$$
By Corollary \ref{L:2.5} we have
$$\ldots=[A_G\otimes_{k}A'_G]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}=[A_G]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}\otimes_{k}[A'_G]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}=\rho'_{\phi}([A_G])\otimes_{k}\rho'_{\phi}([A'_G]),$$
proving that \eqref{prenu} is a group homomorphism. Surjectivity of this homomorphism follows from \cite[Prop. 3]{Kanzaki}.
Let us compute the kernel of $\rho'_{\phi}$.
By \cite[Prop. 5.3]{AMGO}, $[A_G]\in\ker(\rho'_{\phi})$ if and only if $A_G \stackrel{G}{\cong}$ End$_k(P)$  for some faithful progenerator $k$-module $P$.
If the latter holds, then by \cite[Prop. 5(1)]{Kanzaki}, $[P] \in \text{Pic}(K)$, and so by Corollary \ref{L:2.11}, $[A_G]\in\text{Pic}(K)([K_{\phi}G])$. Conversely, suppose that $[A_G]\in\text{Pic}(K)([K_{\phi}G])$.
Then by Corollary \ref{L:2.11}, $A_G\cong{\text{end}}_k(P)$ for some $[P]\in\text{Pic}(K)$. By Lemma \ref{invprogen}
                                                                                                                           
$[A_G]_{{\text{Br}}(k)}$ is trivial, that is $[A_G]\in\ker(\rho'_{\phi})$.
The transition to \eqref{nu} is completed by the identification \eqref{Cliffmod}
between the classes of $[A_G]$ in ${\tilde{\text{Cliff}}(\phi,K)}/_{\mbox{Pic$(K)$}}$ and in ${\tilde{\text{Cliff}}(\phi,K)}/_{\mbox{Pic$(K)([K_{\phi}G])$}}$.

The commutation properties (1) and (2) are established by a direct computation, making use of \cite[Theorem 5.7]{AMGO},
and bearing in mind that all homomorphisms that participate in these two equalities are well-defined.
